newsitem.title: PERU: Peru's Fujimori ponders hostage crisis options.
newsitem.headline: Peru's Fujimori ponders hostage crisis options.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori met with a leading peace broker in Peru's 119-day-old hostage crisis to weigh what concessions to offer Marxist rebels holding 72 captives at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima.
Fujimori and Roman Catholic Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani discussed the standoff for nearly four hours at Government Palace on Monday. Neither made any comment to reporters after the meeting.
Negotiations to persuade about 20 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) gunmen to give up their fight and free the 72 hostages have been kept secret in recent weeks.
But sources close to the talks have said the government is considering some concessions on the MRTA's key demand for the freedom of about 450 jailed rebels.
The sources said the government and the MRTA were engaged in a bartering process to decide which prisoners, if any, might be released.

In spite of a willingness to bargain with the MRTA to avoid bloodshed, Fujimori is unlikely to free any MRTA inmates convicted of violent acts and certainly not any of the group's leaders, the sources added.
The painfully slow pace of the behind-the-scenes negotiations was exasperating the hostages, a doctor said on Monday.

"I found them ... a little worried and desperate that things were not improving and the talks were not progressing," Dr. Miguel Sanchez Palacios, a heart specialist and former hostage, said after visiting the residence.

The rebels originally seized more than 500 guests when they stormed a cocktail party at Japanese Ambassador Morihisa Aoki's home Dec 17. They later released most, hanging on to a select group that includes Aoki and Bolivian Ambassador Jorge Gumucio, two Peruvian government ministers, two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats and Fujimori's younger brother.
Most of the 72 hostages that remain are middle-aged men and many suffer from high blood pressure and heart problems.
Nevertheless, a balanced diet and regular exercise programme had seen some lose weight and even improve their health over the 17 weeks of captivity, Sanchez said.
"Of course not all of them, but a good number, and this means that they need less medication than before," he told local Radioprogramas.
Face-to-face talks between government negotiatior Domingo Palermo and MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini broke off on March 12 and most Peruvian feel the crisis still has along way to run.

A poll of 512 people in Lima published on Monday showed that six out of 10 respondents thought the standoff -- already Latin America's longest -- could drag on for another one to three months or even more.
